Verb structure: SUBJECT–TENSE/ASPECT/POLARITY–VOICE–STEM.

Subject prefixes are aɣa- ‘I’, a- ‘he/it’ and i- ‘they’. These remain present even when a noun subject is stated separately.

Tense/aspect/polarity markers are: no marker for affirmative past, te- for future, b- for ongoing action, ne- for negative past, and se- for negative ongoing/nonpast action.

Voice is unmarked for ordinary active verbs. The prefix t- makes a passive, while s- makes a causative (‘have somebody do something’). The causative prefix harmonizes with a sibilant in the stem: it becomes z- with z and š- with š; consequently, ʒ- is expected with ʒ in iʒuwenket.

Several verbs have different ordinary active and passive/causative stems: gon → elmez ‘swallow’, dini → ubuz ‘take’, kaw → ukuš ‘take out’, dumbu → egzem ‘slaughter’, and nin → išu ‘drink’. Other stems illustrated are egmi ‘look for’, uswud ‘watch’, and efred ‘gather’.

5.1:
a. ‘The water was not drunk.’ anetišu = a-ne-t-išu: third-person singular, negative past, passive, ‘drink’.
b. ‘I had the sheep watched.’ aɣasuswud = aɣa-s-uswud: first-person singular, past, causative, ‘watch’.
c. ‘The salt will be swallowed.’ atetelmez = a-te-t-elmez: third-person singular, future, passive, ‘swallow’.
d. ‘He is not taking the corpse.’ asedini = a-se-dini: third-person singular, negative nonpast, active ‘take’.

5.2:
e. absubuz aryen — absubuz = a-b-s-ubuz: ‘He is having the water taken.’
f. aɣabʒiʒuwenket i — aɣabʒiʒuwenket = aɣa-b-ʒ-iʒuwenket: ‘I’m having them walked.’
g. amanokal anenin aryen — anenin = a-ne-nin: ‘The chief did not drink the water.’
h. cidi anetegmi — anetegmi = a-ne-t-egmi: ‘The salt was not looked for.’
i. atesefred cidi — atesefred = a-te-s-efred: ‘He will have the salt gathered.’

Tadaksahak phrases can have the order subject–verb–object: for example, feji abnin aryen means ‘The sheep is drinking the water.’ A pronominal object follows the verb, as in atedini a ‘He will take it.’ With a passive verb, the affected noun is the subject and precedes the verb: hamu anetubuz means ‘The meat was not taken.’ A third-person subject can also be expressed by the verb without a separate noun.

The verb forms contain a stem together with material indicating the subject, tense or polarity, and whether the action is passive or causative. The examples show:
• aɣa- marks a first-person singular subject: aɣagon ‘I swallowed’ and aɣakaw ‘I took out.’
• i- occurs in affirmative past forms with third-person subjects, as in idumbu ‘they slaughtered.’ Third-person a- occurs in several other forms.
• -te- marks the future in atedini ‘he will take it.’ Another -te- marks passive voice: compare cidi atetegmi ‘the salt will be looked for,’ where both occur, with itegzem ‘they were slaughtered.’
• -ne- marks negation in past forms, as in anetubuz ‘was not taken’; -se- marks negation in present forms, as in asetefred ‘is not being gathered.’
• Causative forms express having somebody perform an action. They contain a consonant such as s, z or š before the stem, as in asegmi ‘he had them looked for,’ atezelmez ‘he will have [it] swallowed,’ and anešišu ‘he did not have [it] drunk.’ The causative material and adjacent vowels vary with the verb form.

Thus aryen anetišu means ‘The water was not drunk’; aɣasuswud feji means ‘I am having the sheep watched’; cidi atetelmez means ‘The salt will be swallowed’; and asedini jifa means ‘He had the corpse taken.’ For the other requested constructions, the same patterns combine a causative with ‘take,’ ‘walk,’ or ‘gather,’ or a past negative with ‘drink’ or passive ‘look for.’ The supplied examples establish these combinations of meanings, though the exact form of every new combination is not independently illustrated.

{"g":"The recurring first words classify things by their shape, substance or type. Comparing phrases with the same second word reveals these patterns:

• daim is used for flat things: daim nplooj is the leaf and daim ntawv the sheet of paper.
• kua indicates liquid: kua mis is milk, whereas lub mis is the breast. Kua txiv hmab is grape juice.
• lub is used for rounded objects: the breast, navel (ntaws), coin (nyiaj) and fruit (txiv).
• phau indicates a stack or collection: phau khaub is the pile of clothes, phau ntawv the book and phau nyiaj the stack of bank notes.
• tsab indicates written communications: tsab ntawv is the postal letter and tsab xov the written message. Zaj xov is the spoken message, suggesting zaj classifies spoken or performed content.
• txoj is used for long, thin things: the vine (hmab), road (kev), nerves (leeg) and umbilical cord (ntaws). The shared ntaws links the navel and umbilical cord. Txoj kev thaj yeeb extends ‘road’ metaphorically to ‘the way of peace’.

These patterns give lub hnub for the sun (rounded), txoj hlua for the rope (long and thin), zaj nkauj for the song (performed content), sau ntawv for the essay (writing), and daim teb for the field (a flat expanse of land). Since txiv means fruit and hmab means vine, the grape is lub txiv hmab, literally a rounded vine-fruit; replacing lub with kua gives grape juice."}

extracted.g:
The recurring first words classify things by their shape, substance or type. Comparing phrases with the same second word reveals these patterns:

• daim is used for flat things: daim nplooj is the leaf and daim ntawv the sheet of paper.
• kua indicates liquid: kua mis is milk, whereas lub mis is the breast. Kua txiv hmab is grape juice.
• lub is used for rounded objects: the breast, navel (ntaws), coin (nyiaj) and fruit (txiv).
• phau indicates a stack or collection: phau khaub is the pile of clothes, phau ntawv the book and phau nyiaj the stack of bank notes.
• tsab indicates written communications: tsab ntawv is the postal letter and tsab xov the written message. Zaj xov is the spoken message, suggesting zaj classifies spoken or performed content.
• txoj is used for long, thin things: the vine (hmab), road (kev), nerves (leeg) and umbilical cord (ntaws). The shared ntaws links the navel and umbilical cord. Txoj kev thaj yeeb extends ‘road’ metaphorically to ‘the way of peace’.

These patterns give lub hnub for the sun (rounded), txoj hlua for the rope (long and thin), zaj nkauj for the song (performed content), sau ntawv for the essay (writing), and daim teb for the field (a flat expanse of land). Since txiv means fruit and hmab means vine, the grape is lub txiv hmab, literally a rounded vine-fruit; replacing lub with kua gives grape juice.

Northern Pame uses base 8: a number is expressed as a multiple of eight followed by the remainder, in the form ‘q tenhiuɲ r’ (= 8q + r). The coefficients 1–3 have special forms: kara, kanuje and karnuʔ.

Central Pame uses base 20: ‘q lien r’ means 20q + r. Within each group of twenty, seskaʔai means 10 and is followed by units to form 11–19. Thus Northern Pame groups numbers in eights, while Central Pame groups them in twenties, with an intermediate grouping of ten.

   - lemonade and the Denver Broncos at **2**
   - hummingbirds and the Audi at **3**
   - the Knicks and bird watching at **4**
   - the Toyota at **5**

   The Mercedes and Salem are at **4**, the Seahawks at **5**, and Blue Master at **6**. Clues 61, 85, and 94 then put coffee at **5** and milk at **6**.

3. Let the pizza position be \(p\). Clues 52 and 118 put Sapphires at \(p-1\) and Opals at \(p+1\); clues 40 and 122 put Amethysts at \(p+2\) and pasta at \(p+3\). Since noodles are at 6, the only possibilities are **\(p=2\)** or **\(p=4\)**.

The remaining clues then put the Warriors at 3 and the BMW/photography at 2. Iced tea must be at 1: it cannot be at 3 because the Warriors are there, or at 4 because humor is there. Water must be at 4 and beer at 3. But cheese making must be next to beer, at 2 or 4—already occupied by photography and bird watching. This is impossible.

5. Thus pizza is at **4**, making Amethysts position **6**. The Dane, who likes Obsidians, is at an end. If Obsidians were at 7, skiing would be at 6, and clue 33 would put Ambers there too, contradicting Amethysts at 6.

Therefore, **Obsidians must be at position 1**.

• f represents [ɸ], r represents [ɾ], and y represents [j]. The other ordinary letters retain their displayed sound values.

• Insert [ʔ] before a word-initial vowel and between adjacent vowels, as in ezi and brüziä. Mark the resulting syllable boundaries with full stops.

items.text:
{"j.":"Tadaksahak verbs have the structure SUBJECT PREFIX + TENSE/POLARITY MARKER + VOICE PREFIX + STEM.

Subject prefixes are aɣa- ‘I’, a- ‘he/it’, and i- ‘they’. The subject prefix remains present when a noun subject is explicitly stated.

Tense/polarity markers are: no marker for affirmative past, b- for affirmative present/progressive, te- for affirmative future, ne- for negative past, and se- for negative present/progressive.

Voice prefixes are: no prefix for active, t- for passive (‘be acted upon’), and s- for causative (‘have somebody act upon something’). The causative prefix agrees with a sibilant in the stem: it becomes z- with elmez and egzem, and š- with ukuš and išu. Thus, with iʒuwenket ‘walk’, it becomes ʒ-.

Several verbs have different active and passive/causative stems: gon / elmez ‘swallow’, dini / ubuz ‘take’, kaw / ukuš ‘take out’, dumbu / egzem ‘slaughter’, and nin / išu ‘drink’. Other stems shown are egmi ‘look for’, uswud ‘watch’, and efred ‘gather’.

Phrase order is subject–verb–object. An independent subject can be omitted because the verb identifies it. Object pronouns follow the verb: a means ‘him/it’, and i means ‘them’. In passive phrases, the affected entity is the subject, preceding the verb. Causative objects likewise follow the verb; the person performing the caused action need not be expressed.

These rules give the following answers to 5.1:
a. ‘The water was not drunk’: a-ne-t-išu.
b. ‘I had the sheep watched’: aɣa-s-uswud.
c. ‘The salt will be swallowed’: a-te-t-elmez.
d. ‘He is not taking the corpse’: a-se-dini.

For 5.2:
e. absubuz aryen — a-b-s-ubuz: ‘He is having the water taken.’
f. aɣabʒiʒuwenket i — aɣa-b-ʒ-iʒuwenket: ‘I’m having them walked.’
g. amanokal anenin aryen — a-ne-nin: ‘The chief did not drink the water.’
h. cidi anetegmi — a-ne-t-egmi: ‘The salt was not looked for.’
i. atesefred cidi — a-te-s-efred: ‘He will have the salt gathered.’"}

Tadaksahak verbs have the structure SUBJECT PREFIX + TENSE/POLARITY MARKER + VOICE PREFIX + STEM.

Subject prefixes are aɣa- ‘I’, a- ‘he/it’, and i- ‘they’. The subject prefix remains present when a noun subject is explicitly stated.

Tense/polarity markers are: no marker for affirmative past, b- for affirmative present/progressive, te- for affirmative future, ne- for negative past, and se- for negative present/progressive.

Voice prefixes are: no prefix for active, t- for passive (‘be acted upon’), and s- for causative (‘have somebody act upon something’). The causative prefix agrees with a sibilant in the stem: it becomes z- with elmez and egzem, and š- with ukuš and išu. Thus, with iʒuwenket ‘walk’, it becomes ʒ-.

Several verbs have different active and passive/causative stems: gon / elmez ‘swallow’, dini / ubuz ‘take’, kaw / ukuš ‘take out’, dumbu / egzem ‘slaughter’, and nin / išu ‘drink’. Other stems shown are egmi ‘look for’, uswud ‘watch’, and efred ‘gather’.

Phrase order is subject–verb–object. An independent subject can be omitted because the verb identifies it. Object pronouns follow the verb: a means ‘him/it’, and i means ‘them’. In passive phrases, the affected entity is the subject, preceding the verb. Causative objects likewise follow the verb; the person performing the caused action need not be expressed.

These rules give the following answers to 5.1:
a. ‘The water was not drunk’: a-ne-t-išu.
b. ‘I had the sheep watched’: aɣa-s-uswud.
c. ‘The salt will be swallowed’: a-te-t-elmez.
d. ‘He is not taking the corpse’: a-se-dini.

For 5.2:
e. absubuz aryen — a-b-s-ubuz: ‘He is having the water taken.’
f. aɣabʒiʒuwenket i — aɣa-b-ʒ-iʒuwenket: ‘I’m having them walked.’
g. amanokal anenin aryen — a-ne-nin: ‘The chief did not drink the water.’
h. cidi anetegmi — a-ne-t-egmi: ‘The salt was not looked for.’
i. atesefred cidi — a-te-s-efred: ‘He will have the salt gathered.’

Subject nouns have two number patterns:
• People and animals: -na singular, -nemą plural.
